q2.answer: In the bone of the upper jaw that holds the teeth, in the gum next to the front teeth. It is called the alveolar cleft.
q2.where: Sheet 1, key message box and 'What this model shows'

q3.answer: The small tooth next to the front tooth (the lateral incisor) never grew. About half of children with a cleft do not have this tooth on the cleft side.

q4.answer: The eye tooth is still up in the bone and leans toward the gap. It needs bone to grow into and come down, so the graft gives it bone to come down into.
q4.where: Sheet 1, 'The eye tooth' and 'Why surgeons do the bone graft'

q5.answer: At about 8 to 11 years old. Teams pick the time by how far the teeth have grown, not by age. The best time is before the eye tooth comes through the gum.

q6.answer: Most often from the hip (soft, spongy bone).

q7.answer: New bone fills the gap and the gum has healed over it. The graft joins the two parts of the upper jaw. The eye tooth is still in the bone but a little lower.
q7.where: Sheet 2, key message box and 'What has changed'

q8.answer: With an X-ray at about 3 to 6 months, which shows how well the new bone has taken.

q9.answer: Your hip can be sore for a while after the bone is taken. In one study, children went back to school about 2 weeks after surgery. I don't know how sore or exactly how long.

q10.answer: It has come down through the new bone and is fully in the row of teeth.
q10.where: Sheet 3, key message box and 'What has changed'

q11.answer: Fixed braces. Almost everyone who has this graft needs them.
q11.where: Sheet 3, key message box and 'What has changed'

q12.answer: Two main plans. Close the space: braces move the eye tooth into the missing tooth's place and the dentist reshapes it, which teams use most often. Keep the space: a removable plate with a false tooth while still growing, then when growth stops an implant (post with a crown) or a bridge (false tooth with one wing glued behind the next tooth). The cleft team will talk with you about which suits you.
